summary.text: 多 is used for “many” and “much.” Early inscriptions already use it with the sense “many.” Its ancient graphic motivation is disputed: early forms are reported as two 肉 (“flesh”) shapes, while later shapes came to resemble 夕; the evidence does not settle whether the picture meant abundance or simply repeated a form.

formation.text: A pictographic compound is the best-supported description of the reported early graph: it was formed from two 肉-like shapes. Whether those shapes specifically represented two pieces of meat to suggest abundance, or conveyed “many” through duplication, remains unresolved. The familiar 夕+夕 analysis is recorded in the Shuowen as a historical explanation, but does not establish the earliest graph’s construction.

components.text: In the reported early graph, this component depicted flesh. The early form is described as 肉; later shapes were visually confused with 夕. Two 肉 shapes are reported, but their intended relation to “many” is uncertain.

In the proposed duplication analysis, this is a second 肉-like pictorial element. The two-shape analysis is disputed, and a one-meat name form complicates it; this account does not establish a separate lexical contribution for this element.

history.text: The curated oracle-script illustration is a modern redraw of a reported early form; it is not an artifact image and cannot by itself identify the shapes or settle the graph’s motivation.

Later bronze and bamboo forms are reported to have become visually confused with 夕, although a 肉-like shape persisted in a bronze form of the 多 component in 宜. The evidence does not establish a dated sequence or the precise point of this graphic change. The Shuowen’s analysis as 重 plus 夕 is a separate historical explanation, not proof of the earliest form.

uncertainties.text: The evidence supports an early two-肉 analysis, but leaves its motivation unresolved: abundance from two pieces of meat and meaning through graphic duplication are proposals, and a one-肉 personal-name form is counterevidence to a simple doubling account.

The cited early inscriptions support “many,” but do not establish an exact date for the individual oracle-bone example or a complete chronology of later senses. Dictionary glosses such as “surpass” and “excess” are not enough to establish when or how those meanings developed.

senses.text: Oracle-bone and bronze inscription contexts are reported with 多 meaning “many”; the cited oracle-bone inscription has no exact date established here.

senses.period: Warring States text; exact date unresolved
senses.text: 多言後 is cited as an adverbial or frequentative use in a Warring States bamboo text. This attestation does not establish a complete path from the “many” sense.
“More than” and “over” are recorded as meanings, but the available evidence does not date this sense or establish its development from “many.”

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish a chronology linking the adverbial use or “more than” to the earliest attested “many” sense.
The cited dictionary lists “surpass,” “excess,” and “praise/esteem,” but the available evidence does not establish their dates or semantic links; they are omitted from the sense sequence.

overview.text: 多 means “many” or “much.” Early forms are reported as two flesh shapes, but scholars have not settled whether they pictured abundant meat or conveyed “many” by repetition.

components.text: This element was represented as flesh in the reported early form; whether the picture meant meat abundance is uncertain.
A second flesh-like element supports the proposed repetition or abundance picture, though a one-flesh name form complicates that analysis.

relationships.text: The early graph is reported as two 肉-like forms; this edge records the first pictorial element in that proposed analysis, whose original motivation remains unsettled.
This separate edge records the proposed second 肉-like element in the two-form analysis; duplication as the source of “many” is disputed.
